theme: I will bless the LORD at all times, taste and see
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 34. This is an acrostic psalm, each verse beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Read it as a testimony and a teaching.
settingTheScene: The title says it was written “when he changed his behavior before Abimelech, so that he drove him out, and he went away.” This refers to the time David feigned madness before King Achish of Gath (1 Samuel 21:10-15). Abimelech seems to be a title or alternate name. Having read that story, notice that David writes a psalm of praise about one of his most embarrassing moments. He saw the hand of God even in that.
observation: “I will bless the LORD at all times; his praise shall continually be in my mouth” (v. 1).
“Oh, magnify the LORD with me, and let us exalt his name together!” (v. 3).
“I sought the LORD, and he answered me and delivered me from all my fears” (v. 4).
“This poor man cried, and the LORD heard him and saved him out of all his troubles” (v. 6).
“The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them” (v. 7).
“Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good! Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him!” (v. 8).
“The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit” (v. 18).
“Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him out of them all” (v. 19).
interpretation:
David turns an embarrassing escape into a hymn. He had acted like a madman, drooling on his beard, to avoid being killed. Yet he does not boast of his cleverness. He credits God: “This poor man cried, and the LORD heard him.” He calls himself poor. He knows he was saved by grace, not by his own wits.

The psalm moves from personal testimony to public invitation. “Magnify the LORD with me.” David wants others to share his joy. A good testimony is not just a story about what God did for me. It is an invitation to see God for who he is.

The famous line, “Taste and see that the LORD is good,” invites experience rather than argument. God is not only to be believed in but tasted. The psalm does not ask for blind faith. It points to the evidence of a life lived under God’s care, and it invites us to test it.

Verse 10 offers a striking contrast: “The young lions suffer want and hunger; but those who seek the LORD lack no good thing.” Lions are the strongest of predators, and yet they go hungry. Those who trust God, though weak, lack nothing that is truly good.

The center of the psalm’s teaching is verse 18: “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted.” It is one of the most comforting promises in the Bible. God is not distant from those who suffer. He is near. And verse 19 is honest: “Many are the afflictions of the righteous.” The psalm does not promise a life without trouble. It promises deliverance from it all.

The final verse offers a guarantee: “The LORD redeems the life of his servants; none of those who take refuge in him will be condemned.”
connection: John 19:36 applies verse 20 to Jesus: “Not one of his bones will be broken.” Peter quotes verses 12 to 16 in 1 Peter 3:10-12 to teach Christians how to live. 1 Peter 2:3 echoes “taste and see” (“if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good”). Jesus is the “angel of the LORD” fulfilled in the sense that he is near to those who are crushed (Matthew 11:28-30). Romans 8:1 says there is no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus.
application:
Turn an embarrassing or painful memory into a testimony of God’s help.

Today, “taste and see.” Look for a specific way that God shows his goodness.

Reach out to someone who is brokenhearted and be near to them.
prayerPrompts: Bless the LORD at this moment, in your own words.
Thank him for answering you in the past.
Pray for someone brokenhearted, and thank him that he is near.
